title: Analyzing Earnings Calls
text:
Today


Where earnings call transcripts come from, and what they cost
A question: can a model read a call and tell you to buy?
How fast you would have to act on the answer
Directions we could take it

title: Analyzing Earnings Calls
text:
Transcripts, Free


Motley Fool
The archive, scraped. 2021 to now, roughly 45,000 calls. Prepared remarks and Q&A in full.


EarningsCall
Clean API, good SDK. The free tier is two companies: Apple and Microsoft.


SEC EDGAR
8-K Item 2.02 is the press release, not the call. Public domain, timestamped to the second.



The Fool archive paginates at 50 pages, about three weeks. The monthly sitemap has no cap and is how you reach 2021.

title: Analyzing Earnings Calls
text:
Transcripts, Paid







EarningsCall
9,000+ companies, speaker-segmented, MIT-licensed SDK


Financial Modeling Prep
transcripts on a paid tier; you may already hold a key


API Ninjas
one endpoint, history to 2000, premium below 2026


Capital IQ via WRDS
the research standard, 2004 on, ~5,000 US firms




Rice does not subscribe to Capital IQ Transcripts. ciq_transcripts returns permission denied; the sample is 20 calls from 2005.

title: Analyzing Earnings Calls
text:
The Other Half: Labels


Free and current
Yahoo for returns, Finnhub for consensus. Current to yesterday. Runs in your container.

Research grade, but stale
CRSP daily ends 2025-12-31. The market index file ends 2024-12-31. IBES ends 2026-05-14.


WRDS cannot label a call from last month. That is not a small detail; it decides which sample you can study.

title: Analyzing Earnings Calls
section: Can a Model Read a Call and Tell You to Buy?
text:
Can a Model Read a Call and Tell You to Buy?

A transcript is 43,000 characters of management telling you how the quarter went. Somewhere in there is information about what the stock is worth.


The question is not whether a model can summarize it. It obviously can. The question is whether anything it produces survives contact with a price.

title: Analyzing Earnings Calls
section: How Fast Would We Have to Act?
text:
How Fast Would We Have to Act?

The call is public the moment it ends. Our transcripts are not.



4 days median lag, call to Fool transcript


53% posted 3+ days after the call


5 min what the professionals allow themselves



Measured on 449 of our own transcripts. Anything that trades on the announcement itself is gone before we can read it.

title: Analyzing Earnings Calls
text:
Where the Move Actually Is

So the announcement day is out of reach. Is that where the money was?










mean absolute move
is it predictable?




Announcement day
8.1%
yes, partly. R-squared 0.05 on the surprise alone


Next 60 days
17.3%
not from the surprise. R-squared 0.001




Two thirds of the movement happens after the day we cannot trade. None of it that we know how to forecast. Size and predictability are different things.

title: Analyzing Earnings Calls
text:
Four Architectures


Fine-tune
Train a model on transcripts paired with the subsequent price move. End to end, no features.


Extract, then model
The LLM reads the call and emits numbers. A separate ML model turns those into a recommendation.


Embed
Turn the transcript into a vector. Use the vector as a feature list.


Just ask
One prompt, one answer. The thing all three of the above have to beat.

title: Analyzing Earnings Calls
text:
Fine-Tuning

Show a model thousands of transcripts and what the stock did next, and let it find its own features.



For
Nobody has to guess which features matter. The model is optimized for the actual target.

Against
Expensive, hard to interpret, and easy to overfit. What did it learn? You cannot read it off.

title: Analyzing Earnings Calls
text:
Extract, Then Model

The model scores the call on dimensions you define. A regression turns those scores into a position.


Guidance revision, margin durability, how much management hedges, whether the quarter leans on one-off items.


The appeal is that the middle layer is inspectable. When it works you can say which dimension carried it; when it fails you can see where.

title: Analyzing Earnings Calls
text:
Embeddings

Skip the judgment. Turn the whole transcript into a few hundred numbers and regress on those.



Cheap
Orders of magnitude less than generation. You can embed the whole corpus.


Opaque
Dimension 137 is not “margin pressure.” There is nothing to put on a slide.

title: Analyzing Earnings Calls
text:
Just Ask It

Give the model the transcript and ask for a number. No features, no fitting, no training.


This is the control, and it is the one experiment nobody wants to run. If a one-line prompt does as well as a fine-tuned model, that is the result, and it is worth knowing before you spend a week on the alternative.

title: Analyzing Earnings Calls
text:
Three More Angles


Remarks vs Q&A
The prepared remarks are scripted. The Q&A is not. Split the document and see which half carries the signal.


Change, not level
Some CEOs always sound confident. Compare a call to the same firm’s last call and score what moved.


Model as analyst
Ask it what to look for rather than what to conclude. Then test its hypotheses yourself.

title: Analyzing Earnings Calls
text:
What I Already Know

Preliminary, one month, 181 to 198 events. Enough to steer you, not enough to believe.








Announcement-day reaction
ten extracted features added R-squared 0.096 over the surprise, p = 0.007


60-day drift
nothing. Would need roughly 80x the sample to see a 2% effect


Volatility, level
64% explained by its own past. No room


Volatility, change
benchmark only 0.058, and the obvious predictors are exhausted

title: Analyzing Earnings Calls
text:
Your Turn


Pick a direction. Argue for it before you start building.
Decide what your prediction would have to beat, and write that down first.
Build the smallest version that could produce a number.
Tuesday: what you tried, what it gave you, and whether you believe it.



The infrastructure is in the repo: transcripts, extraction, labels, scoring. Take what helps and ignore the rest.

title: Train, Test, and an App
text:
How the Model Was Fit


Use 2001-01 through 2020-12 as the training period.
Filter to approximate Russell 2000 universe - market cap between 1,001 and 3000, inclusive, at the beginning of each month.
Replace every feature with its rank (0 to 1) inside that month’s Russell 2000 universe.
Choose the hyperparameters on expanding-window folds: train on the earliest months, validate on the block that follows.
Refit on the whole training period with the chosen settings and save the model to a file: session7_model.joblib.



Industry is not a feature: an earlier fit with sector dummies picked up the sector returns of the training years.

title: Train, Test, and an App
text:
Target and Scoring

Try to predict how each stock’s return will rank in the Russell 2000 universe, from 0 to 1.
Not trying to predict whether stocks are up or down in aggregate — no market timing.
Just trying to predict which stocks will beat others.
For evaluating hyperparameters, rank predictions 0 to 1 and compute correlation with actual ranks. Higher ecorrelation is better.

title: Train, Test, and an App
text:
Expanding-Window Folds

The 240 training months are cut into six blocks of 40. Each fold trains on the blocks before it and is scored on the one that follows.

block      1      2      3      4      5      6
fold 1   train  valid
fold 2   train  train  valid
fold 3   train  train  train  valid
fold 4   train  train  train  train  valid
fold 5   train  train  train  train  train  valid

Six blocks give five folds. The folds are whole months and always run forward — shuffling the rows would train the model on 2018 to predict 2006.

title: Train, Test, and an App
text:
Test Procdure

session7_test.parquet contains the 15 features ranked within each cross section 2001-01 through 2026-09
Applying session7_model.joblib to each cross-section gives predictions (of ranks)
Assignment was to form portfolios based on the predictions and to evaluate the results

title: Train, Test, and an App
text:
Refit on All Past Data

The expanding-window cross-validation was repeated on the full dataset 2001-01 through 2026-09
Using the best hyperparameters, the model was refit on the full dataset: session7_model_full.joblib

title: Train, Test, and an App
section: Use the Model to Make Predictions
text:
Use the Model to Make Predictions

Our goal is to use it to make stock predictions for the upcoming month (21 trading days)
We should update our features daily based on prices and volumes and any new 10-K’s
Instead we are going to use data frozen last week: session7_live.parquet

title: Train, Test, and an App
text:
Frontend and Backend


Frontend
The browser. HTML, CSS, and JavaScript — it draws the page and collects the clicks.

Backend
A program on a server that listens continuously for requests. Yours will be Python.


You open a URL. The browser sends a GET request. The server sends back the HTML, CSS, and JavaScript it was written to send. The browser interprets that and shows you a page.


Right-click any web page and choose View Page Source. That is the frontend code, exactly as the backend handed it over.

title: Train, Test, and an App
text:
Then You Click Something

A POST request carries data the other way — a form, a ticker you typed. The server does what it was written to do and replies.

title: Train, Test, and an App
text:
Running Locally

The backend and the frontend can be the same computer — lab638, or your own laptop if you have Python installed on it.



localhost
127.0.0.1 is the loopback address. The browser asks the machine it is already running on, and the request never reaches a network.


Ports
One machine can run many programs listening at once. The port number tells the operating system which of them gets the request.



You write the app as a .py file. FastAPI is the dominant Python library for writing one; uvicorn runs it and starts it listening on a port: python3 -m uvicorn app:app --reload.

title: Train, Test, and an App
text:
Basic Design


The fitted gradient boosting model session7_model_full.joblib is baked into the app (rebuild the app when the model is refitted)
Overnight, all new data should be pulled, ranks computed, the model run, and predictions made
The predictions should be mapped into whatever output you want the app to have (Buy, Sell, etc.)
User inputs a ticker and gets the output
We’re going to skip the overnight pulling and bake session7_live.parquet into the app

title: Train, Test, and an App
section: First, What do the Predictions Look Like?
text:
First, What do the Predictions Look Like?

Every prediction sits between 0.448 and 0.518. Adjacent decile cutoffs in the middle are four thousandths apart.

title: Train, Test, and an App
text:
What the App Should Produce

First, where does a stock fit within the predictions? Top decile? Middle quintile? …
Where does it fit within its sector or industry?
Within a marketcap band? (But only small caps here).


Argue these out with AI before you ask it to write code.

title: Train, Test, and an App
text:
Platform as a Service

You hand a host your repository. It builds the app, runs it, and puts it behind a public URL — there is no server for you to administer. Railway, Render, Koyeb, and Heroku all do this. We will use Koyeb, which has a free tier.



Create a free account at koyeb.com.
In the control panel, create an API access token. Koyeb shows it once, so copy it then.
In a terminal, add it to your .env file:


printf '\nKOYEB_ACCESS_TOKEN=your_access_token\n' >> $HOME/.env

>> appends, and creates the file if you do not have one. Koyeb’s web UI will link a GitHub repo with no token at all — the token is what lets AI do the deploying for you, which is the path we are taking.

title: Train, Test, and an App
text:
Deploy the App


Prompt

My goal is to push this app to GitHub as a new public repo and then create a Koyeb service connected to that repo. Walk me through it one step at a time.


On day one you told git to ignore parquet files. The host builds only what is in the repo, so the model file and the data the app reads have to get there. And nothing from .env belongs in a public repo — secrets go in Koyeb’s environment settings.

title: Train, Test, and an App
text:
Get a Custom Domain

Optional. The Koyeb URL works fine on its own.



Create an account at dnsimple.com and buy a domain name.
In your DNSimple account settings, create an API access token and add it to .env:


printf '\nDNSIMPLE_ACCESS_TOKEN=your_access_token\n' >> $HOME/.env


Prompt

I bought mydomain.com at DNSimple and my app is running on Koyeb. Use the DNSimple API v2 with DNSIMPLE_ACCESS_TOKEN to create the record Koyeb needs, and tell me what to configure on the Koyeb side.

title: Linear Regression for Multiples
text:
The Moves


Winsorize
Clip each variable at its 1st and 99th percentile. Keeps the company, discards the magnitude.


Standardize
Subtract the mean, divide by the standard deviation. Puts every variable on the same scale.


Log
Take logs. Converts right-skewed distributions (marketcap, household income, …) into more symmetric ones.



They are not interchangeable, and only two of the three will do anything to an OLS R-squared.

title: Linear Regression for Multiples
text:
Machine Learning

Machine learning deals with the following type of situation.


In the future, I will have some data. I want to use it to make a prediction about another variable.
I also have past data on the predictors (x variables) and the dependent variable (y).
I want to build a model using the past data that predicts y from the x variables.
In the future, I will use the model to make predictions.


What machine learning cares about is how well a model trained (fitted) on past data will perform on future data. This is out-of-sample performance, because the future x’s and y are not part of the sample used to build the model.

title: Linear Regression for Multiples
text:
Train-Test Split

To assess expected out-of-sample performance, we withhold some of our current data when training. We use the held-out data to test the model.



Ask AI to use scikit-learn to do a train-test split, to transform features (x variables) on the training data, apply the same transformations on the test data, and determine goodness of fit on the test data.
Ask AI to create an html doc explaining what was done and explaining the performance on the test data.

title: Linear Regression for Multiples
text:
Assignment for Tuesday

Can we trade on this? Use session4_monthly.parquet. In each row, everything except the return is known at the beginning of the month.



Run a linear regression each month, using some multiple on the left-hand side. Use scikit-learn, but do not use train-test splits. Our test will be whether we make money.
Sort stocks each month based on the regression error. If the left-hand side is ps, or log ps, then positive errors (ps > predicted) are expensive firms. You would want to buy stocks with the “most negative” errors.
Form a portfolio each month and compute its return. Evaluate the returns of the strategy — annualized mean, Sharpe ratio, CAPM alpha, …



Be prepared to present on Tuesday — slides if you want them but be prepared to dig into the analysis.

title: Median of Peer Multiples
text:
Value It Four Ways


Fix the peer set — same industry, same size bucket, same date — and count it
Take the median of each of the four multiples across those peers
Multiply each median by the company’s own denominator
For EV/EBITDA, cross back from enterprise value to equity



Four implied equity values for one company. Compare each with the market cap it actually trades at.

title: Median of Peer Multiples
text:
What a P/E of –12 Means

Nothing. It means the company lost money.


A negative P/E is not a cheap stock. It is a stock with no E. Left in the sample it drags the median in the wrong direction and makes the cheapest-looking companies the ones losing the most.

EV/EBITDA fails the same way on negative EBITDA. P/B is close to meaningless where the assets walk out of the building at six o’clock — and it means something else again for a bank, where the balance sheet is the business. P/S always exists, which is not the same as always meaning something.

Filter out the negative values. We won’t try to value them or to use them for valuing others.

title: Median of Peer Multiples
text:
Why the Median


The mean
One company with a P/E of 900 — a real company that barely broke even — and the average for the industry is meaningless.

The median
Unmoved by the tail. With ratios, where the numerator is bounded below and the denominator can approach zero, this is not a refinement. It is the difference between a number and noise.


Report the count alongside every median. A median of four is a different object from a median of four hundred, and the table does not tell you which you have.

title: Median of Peer Multiples
text:
Deviations

Deviation = log( market cap / implied value ).

Positive means the market pays more for this company than its peers say it is worth. Negative means the company is cheap compared to peers.

An AI Environment for the Course


What runs

What is installed

What you see
A file browser, a terminal, and a browser view for anything you build.

Sign In

Username is your netid, the part before @rice.edu
Password is your student number, including the S0



First load takes a moment while your machine starts. If you are asked to sign in again later in the term, nothing is wrong — sessions do not survive a restart of the server.

title: 1. Course Introduction

The Workspace


Right panel
Claude Code. The prompt window is at the bottom.


Left panel
File browser by default. Terminal and View are there too — ignore them today.


Three dots, upper left
Upload from your laptop, download to it.

title: 1. Course Introduction
text:
Things to Remember







Refresh
The file browser does not update itself. When GLM makes a file and you cannot see it, hit Refresh.


No Office
Double-clicking a .xlsx or .pptx does nothing. Office is not installed.


Download to view
Bring Office documents to your laptop and open them there.

title: 1. Course Introduction
text:
Good Enough Prompting

Most of the prompt engineering advice from a few years ago is now either useless or actively harmful.



Say what you want, not how to do it
“I want to compare revenue across countries — how should we show it?”
beats
“Make a bar chart, sorted descending, gridlines off, 12pt labels.”


If it does not work, try again
Rephrasing is cheap. Treat it as an infinitely patient colleague with a poor memory.

title: 1. Course Introduction
text:
Plan Before You Act
Say: plan how to do this before you start.


Why it works — knowledge
Planning pulls the relevant considerations into the conversation. It then answers in light of what it just retrieved.

Why it works — subtasks
It breaks the work into steps you can check one at a time. Failures stay small and local instead of surfacing at the very end.

title: 1. Course Introduction
text:
Confirm It Understood

Ambiguity does not produce a question. It produces a confident answer to a question you did not ask.

Tell GLM, before it starts

Tell me what you are about to do and what you are assuming.


Correct it in one sentence, then say go ahead. This is the cheapest habit in the course and it will save you the most time.

title: 1. Course Introduction
section: It Is a Prediction Machine, Not a Colleague
text:
It Is a Prediction Machine, Not a Colleague
Suppose it told you last week that method A beats method B. Today you ask it to do the task.


What it will do
If “A beats B” is not in this conversation, and B appeared more often in its training data, it will probably use B.

Why
Knowledge in the weights is not knowledge in use. Something has to pull it into the conversation before it can act on it.

title: 1. Course Introduction
text:
Tunnel Vision

Prediction also means momentum. Once it has started down a path, continuing that path is the likeliest next step.

You will watch it hit a roadblock, find a way around, hit another, find another way around — tenaciously, exhaustively. What it rarely does is go back and ask whether a different path was better all along.

Restate the goal, not the obstacle. That gives it permission to abandon the path instead of defending it.

title: 1. Course Introduction
text:
What Not to Do







Skip
Why




“Think step by step”
Reasoning models already do, in hidden tokens


“Take a deep breath”
Measurably useless now


“CRITICAL! NEVER EVER …”
Overtriggers, and gets worse results


Stacked personas
“You are an expert X” can help tone; three of them does not




Direct task framing wins. Say what you want, say what done looks like, say what to avoid.

title: 1. Course Introduction
text:
Anatomy of a Chatbot


You


↔︎


Chatbot


↔︎


The model


The model reads text and writes text. That is the entire capability.

It cannot open a file, run a calculation, look up today’s price, or check whether what it just told you is true.

title: 1. Course Introduction
section: An Agent Is a Chatbot with Tools
text:
An Agent Is a Chatbot with Tools


Code execution


↕


You


↔︎


Agent


↔︎


The model


↕


Other tools



The model never runs any of it — it only emits requests.

title: 1. Course Introduction
text:
The Loop, Step by Step


The agent sends the prompt, the history, and a list of tools it has
The model answers: use tool X, with these arguments
The agent runs tool X and reports the result back, with instructions for reading it
The model decides what to do next — another tool, or an answer for you



The model emits requests; the agent executes them. Those step-3 instructions are the tool harness, and some are far better than others.

title: 1. Course Introduction
text:
Writing and Running Code

Almost everything useful the model does, it does by writing code and running it, including terminal commands.


On our AI lab, GLM will write code, save it to a file (a tool use), then run it with a terminal command (another tool use), read the output (another tool use), and revise and repeat as necessary.

All of this is orchestrated by the Claude Code “harness.”

Excel workbooks with live formulas


Charts and figures


Word and PowerPoint files


Data analysis and statistics


Web apps and dashboards

title: 1. Course Introduction
section: Git Is a Version Control System
text:
Git Is a Version Control System

A commit is a snapshot of the whole folder, dated and labelled. Nothing is ever overwritten — it is added to.


Every commit is a point you can go back to, and Git can tell you what changed between any two of them, in which file, and on which line.

Git is not an AI tool. It is twenty years older than any of this. GLM simply knows how to drive it.

title: 1. Course Introduction
text:
Git vs GitHub


Git
On your machine. The history lives in the folder itself — no network, no account, yours alone.

GitHub
A hosted copy of that same history for backup and sharing.

title: 1. Course Introduction
section: Create an Account and Log In from the Lab
text:
Create an Account and Log In from the Lab


Create a free account at github.com, and note your username
Open the Terminal tab, not the GLM pane — this step waits for you to type
Run gh auth login and answer: GitHub.com, HTTPS, yes to authenticating Git, browser
It prints a code — open the link on your laptop and paste it there

section: One Person in Each Group Does This

One Person in Each Group Does This
Tell GLM — one person in the group, once

Make a folder in my workspace called [whatever you want to call it] and make it a git repository.
Add a .gitignore for csv, parquet, and .env files.
Commit, then create a private GitHub repo of the same name and push to it.

Then Add Your Groupmates
On github.com, in the new repository

Everyone Else Joins

Clone the GitHub repo [username]/[repo name] into my workspace.


username should be the username of the group member who created it. repo name is the name they used for the folder

title: 1. Course Introduction

Later: Push and Pull
Tell GLM, at the start of every session

Pull the latest from GitHub before we start.

Then, at the end of the session

Commit what we did and push it.

title: 1. Course Introduction
text:
When Git Pushes Back







What you see
What to say




rejected --- non-fast-forward
Someone pushed while you were working. “Pull their work, merge it, then push.”


CONFLICT: automatic merge failed
You both edited the same lines. “Show me both versions and wait for me to choose.”




Refuse these if asked: git push --force and git reset --hard

title: Trading on Predictions
text:
Starting Today


Three groups, drawn at random, at the start of every class
Five minutes each, on what you got done last session
Show the repository — the skill, the code, the numbers



What broke is more interesting than what worked, and it is what the rest of the room needs to hear. A presentation that reports only success is a presentation nobody learns from.

title: Trading on Predictions
text:
What to Cover


What you decided
Which multiple, which peer group, what minimum size. And why.


What surprised you
The company where the answer was obviously wrong, and what it turned out to be.


What you would change
You have run it now. What is the first thing you would do differently?

title: Trading on Predictions
section: You Have a Number for Every Stock
text:
You Have a Number for Every Stock

Own P/E divided by peer median P/E. Below one is cheap relative to its peers; above one is expensive.


That is a prediction, whether or not you meant it as one. It says: this company should trade closer to its peers than it does.

The question today is whether that prediction is worth anything.

title: Trading on Predictions
text:
Sort, Do Not Threshold


A threshold
“Buy anything below 0.7.” How many stocks is that? Some years, none. Some years, four hundred.


A sort
“Buy the cheapest tenth.” Always the same number of positions, whatever the market is doing.



Ranking also throws away the scale of the signal, which is the part you trust least. You are betting on the order, not the magnitude.

title: Trading on Predictions
text:
Long, Short, or Both


Long only
Buy the cheapest decile. Most of what you earn is just the market.


Long-short
Cheapest decile long, most expensive short. What is left is the signal.


Long-short, dollar neutral
Equal dollars each side. The version we will build.



The long-short version is a much harder test, and it is the one that tells you whether you found anything.

title: Trading on Predictions
text:
The Loop


Pick a date — the last trading day of June, say
Compute the signal for every stock, using only what was known that day
Sort, and form the portfolio
Hold it for one year. No trading, no rebalancing
Record the return
Move forward a year and do it again



Twenty-odd repetitions. That is your entire sample, and it is worth remembering how small a number that is.

title: Trading on Predictions
text:
Why Once a Year


The signal moves slowly
It is built from annual filings. Recomputing it monthly gives you eleven months of the same answer and eleven months of trading costs.

And it keeps the test honest
Annual holding periods make the overlapping-returns problem go away. Monthly rebalancing with annual data does not give you twelve times the evidence.

title: Trading on Predictions
text:
Equal or Value Weighted


Equal weighted
Same dollars in each name. Simple, and dominated by small companies — which is where most anomalies live, and where they are hardest to trade.


Value weighted
Weights by market cap. A much more honest test, and usually a much weaker result.



Report both. A strategy that works equal-weighted and dies value-weighted has told you exactly what it is.

title: Trading on Predictions
text:
Build It
Tell GLM

Write a backtest. For each year from 2001 to 2025: on June 30, compute the peer-median signal for every stock using the valuation skill, sort into deciles, go long the cheapest decile and short the most expensive, equal weighted, hold twelve months, and record the return. Plan it before you start.


Then read the plan before you let it write anything.

title: Trading on Predictions
text:
The Restatement Problem

MRY is the most recent restatement. It tells you today what nobody knew then.


A company that restated its 2008 earnings in 2011 shows up in MRY with the restated number — so a backtest that forms a 2009 portfolio is using information from 2011. The strategy will look better than it was.

Use the as-reported dimensions, ARY and ARQ, for anything historical.

title: Trading on Predictions
text:
Filed, Not Ended


reportperiod
When the fiscal year ended. Nobody outside the company knew the numbers yet.


datekey
When it was filed with the SEC. This is the first day you could have acted on it.



Sorting on reportperiod gives you a few weeks to a few months of free information, every year, in every name. It is the single most common way a backtest in this course goes wrong.

title: Trading on Predictions
text:
Who Is in the Sample

Ask a question you cannot answer from the schema: does the data still contain companies that stopped existing?


If it holds only companies listed today, then every 2005 portfolio you form is made of firms you already know survived to 2026. That is not a small bias. It is the difference between a strategy and an illusion.

Tell GLM

Count distinct tickers with data in 2005. Then count how many of those still have data in the most recent year, and show me some that do not.

title: Trading on Predictions
text:
Three More







The peer median
Computed from the same date, or from data that arrived later?


Delisting returns
A company that goes to zero has to be recorded as going to zero


Costs and borrow
The short side is not free, especially in the small names




None of these will throw an error. Each of them makes the answer better than the truth.

title: Trading on Predictions
text:
Three Numbers


Average return
The mean of your annual long-short returns.


Standard deviation
How much those returns bounced around, year to year.


The ratio, and its t-stat
With twenty-five observations, the t-stat is doing a lot of work.



Twenty-five annual returns is a small sample. A strategy earning four percent a year with fifteen percent volatility is not distinguishable from nothing.

title: Trading on Predictions
text:
Compare It to Something

Four percent a year is a fact about your strategy. It is not yet a finding.



The market
Did the long side simply do what stocks did?


A random sort
Run it with the signal shuffled. What does noise earn in your backtest?


Value itself
Plain P/E, no peer group. Did the peer adjustment add anything?



The third comparison is the real test of last session’s work.

title: Trading on Predictions
text:
Look at the Years
Tell GLM

Plot the annual return of the long-short portfolio, year by year. Mark the best and worst years and tell me what the portfolio held in each.


An average built out of one enormous year and twenty-four small negative ones is a different animal from a steady four percent, and the summary statistics will not tell you which you have.

title: Trading on Predictions
text:
Three People, No Shared Memory

The conversation you had with GLM on Tuesday is invisible to your groupmates, and gone to you.


The code survives. The reasoning does not — why you used ARY, which peer definition you rejected, what you tried on the short side that did not work. That is exactly what the next person needs, and exactly what nobody writes down.

title: Trading on Predictions
text:
What a Memory File Is


One file per session
Dated, in the repository, next to the code it describes.


Written by GLM
At the end of the session, from the conversation it just had. You correct it.


Read by GLM
At the start of the next session, before it touches anything.



It serves your groupmates and it serves the model. Both start every session knowing nothing.

title: Trading on Predictions
text:
What Goes in It


Date, and who was working
What we set out to do
What we decided, and what we rejected — with the reason
What broke, and whether it is fixed
What is unfinished, and where to pick it up



Point 3 is the one that matters and the one that gets dropped. A decision without its reason gets re-litigated in two weeks.

title: Trading on Predictions
text:
Build the Skill
Tell GLM

Make a skill that writes a session memory file. It should trigger when I say we are wrapping up. Write to memory/YYYY-MM-DD.md with those five headings, drawn from this conversation. Keep it under a page.

Then a second one, or a line in CLAUDE.md:

At the start of every session, read the three most recent files in memory/.

title: Trading on Predictions
text:
Try It Now


Build the skill
Say: we are wrapping up
Read what it wrote — and fix what it got wrong about your own afternoon
Commit and push, so the other two can read it before Thursday



Step 3 is not optional. A memory file nobody checked is a confident record of a session that did not happen.

title: Trading on Predictions
text:
Three Things


Get the backtest running end to end, however crude
Re-run it with ARY and datekey, and record what changed
Write the memory file, and push it



Thursday we stop borrowing the peer median and start predicting the multiple — which turns valuation into a regression, and gives you something to compare today’s result against.

title: Ridge, Lasso, and Trees
section: Empirical Asset Pricing via Machine Learning
text:
Empirical Asset Pricing via Machine Learning

The Review of Financial Studies, February 2020.



Shihao Gu
Booth School of Business, University of Chicago


Bryan Kelly
Yale University; Head of Machine Learning, AQR


Dacheng Xiu
Booth School of Business, University of Chicago



A horse race: one task, one dataset, a dozen methods scored side by side. Predict next month’s return for every U.S. stock from roughly 900 signals — 94 firm characteristics, their interactions with eight macro series, and industry dummies — and grade each method by out-of-sample \(R^2\). Trees and neural networks win, and the gains come from interactions a linear model cannot see. A value-weighted long-short decile spread on the neural network forecasts earns an out-of-sample Sharpe ratio of 1.35.

title: Ridge, Lasso, and Trees
text:
Today


Ridge and lasso — linear regression with a penalty on the coefficients
Hyperparameters
Cross validation
Regression trees and gradient boosting
Predicting a multiple from characteristics

title: Ridge, Lasso, and Trees
text:
Today’s Example

We will use session4.parquet to predict the log of the price-to-sales ratio.




grossmargin
gross margin


ebitdamargin
EBITDA margin


netmargin
net margin


assetturnover
asset turnover


rndint
R&D / sales


currentratio
current ratio


growth
sales growth


de
debt / equity

title: Ridge, Lasso, and Trees
text:
Root Mean Squared Error

A standard deviation measures spread around a mean. RMSE measures spread around a prediction, and it is the same arithmetic.



Standard deviation of a sample
\[s_x \;=\; \sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(x_i - \bar{x}\right)^{2}}\]

Root mean squared error
\[\text{RMSE} \;=\; \sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(y_i - \hat{y}_i\right)^{2}}\]


Each point’s own prediction \(\hat{y}_i\) takes the place of the one number \(\bar{x}\).

title: Ridge, Lasso, and Trees
text:
R-Squared

The squared error you removed, over the squared error you started with.

\[R^{2} \;=\; \frac{\dfrac{1}{n}\sum_{i}\left(y_i - \bar{y}\right)^{2} \;-\; \dfrac{1}{n}\sum_{i}\left(y_i - \hat{y}_i\right)^{2}}{\dfrac{1}{n}\sum_{i}\left(y_i - \bar{y}\right)^{2}}\]
\[R^{2} \;=\; \frac{\text{variance} \;-\; \text{mean squared error}}{\text{variance}}\]

title: Ridge, Lasso, and Trees
text:
One Small Example

Every app today is fitted to the same 40 firms and scored on the same 120, all with market cap above $2b.


Forty is small on purpose. Everything that goes wrong with a thousand features and ten thousand rows goes wrong here too, and here you can watch it happen.

title: Ridge, Lasso, and Trees
text:
What OLS Is Doing

Pick the coefficients that make the sum of squared errors on the training data as small as possible. Nothing else is asked of them.



0.68 train R-squared


0.44 test R-squared


8 features, 40 firms



The fit was chosen to make the first number large. The second is what it is worth on firms it has not seen.

title: Ridge, Lasso, and Trees
text:
Multi-Collinearity

Net margin and EBITDA margin have a correlation of 0.82 across these firms. Least squares is asked which of them explains P/S, and the data cannot say.





OLS coefficient




net margin
+0.63


EBITDA margin
−0.27




A large positive on one and a negative on its near-twin.

title: Ridge, Lasso, and Trees
text:
The Ridge Criterion
\[\min_{\beta} \; \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left( y_i - \beta_0 - \sum_j \beta_j x_{ij} \right)^{2} \;+\; \lambda \sum_j \beta_j^{2}\]


The second term
A price on size. Large coefficients now have to earn their keep.


Standardize first
One penalty for all the coefficients only works if the features share a scale.


Not the intercept
\(\beta_0\) is left out of the sum. Shrinking it would just move the whole fit.



\(\lambda\) is a hyperparameter — a number you set before fitting, rather than one the fitting picks for you. The \(\beta\)’s are parameters and come out of the data; \(\lambda\) decides how hard the data has to argue for them.

title: Ridge, Lasso, and Trees
text: Ridge

title: Ridge, Lasso, and Trees
text:
What the Slider Showed


Everything shrinks
Toward zero, together. At \(\lambda = 0\) the fit is exactly OLS; the gold ticks are where it started.


The twins converge
+0.63 and −0.27 become +0.15 and +0.13. Ridge splits the credit rather than picking a winner.


Nothing reaches zero
Ridge shrinks every coefficient and drops none. All eight features stay in the model.



Test R-squared climbs from 0.44 to 0.66 and then falls away again. The training R-squared drops the whole way.

title: Ridge, Lasso, and Trees
text:
The Lasso Criterion
\[\min_{\beta} \; \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left( y_i - \beta_0 - \sum_j \beta_j x_{ij} \right)^{2} \;+\; \lambda \sum_j \left| \beta_j \right|\]

One character different, and the behavior is not the same. Squaring makes the penalty on a small coefficient negligible; the absolute value does not.


A coefficient that is not paying for itself is pushed all the way to zero and stays there.

title: Ridge, Lasso, and Trees
text:
The Shape of the Penalty


Near zero the square has nothing left to charge; the absolute value still charges full price.

title: Ridge, Lasso, and Trees
text: Lasso

title: Ridge, Lasso, and Trees
text:
How a Tree Fits


Search every feature and every cut point for the one split that reduces the sum of squared errors the most.
Cut the sample in two on that rule.
Repeat inside each piece, and inside the pieces of those pieces.
Predict the average of the training firms that land in each final piece.



No linear form is assumed, so a tree handles a kink or a threshold that a regression has to be told about. The next two slides use gross margin and net margin, because two is the most you can draw.

title: Ridge, Lasso, and Trees
text:
Splitting on Two Features


Each cut is chosen over both variables at once. The winner is whichever single line, in whichever variable, increases the training \(R^2\) the most.

title: Ridge, Lasso, and Trees
text:
One Tree


The boxes and the tree are the same object. A path down the tree is a box; a leaf’s colour is the average of the firms that landed in it.

title: Ridge, Lasso, and Trees
text:
Hyperparameters to Control Overfitting


Max depth
How many cuts deep the tree may go. Depth \(d\) allows up to \(2^d\) leaves; depth 8 here gives 28 boxes for 40 firms.


Minimum per leaf
The smallest number of training points a leaf may hold. A leaf of one is a memorized observation.



At depth 2 the tree scores 0.57 on the training firms and 0.29 on the test firms. At depth 8 it scores 0.96 and \(-0.14\) — worse than a flat line at the average.

title: Ridge, Lasso, and Trees
text:
The Idea


Start by predicting the training mean for everyone.
Compute the residuals — what the current prediction is missing.
Fit a small tree to the residuals.
Add a fraction of that tree, the learning rate, to the prediction.
Go back to step 2.



No single tree is any good. The sum of a few hundred deliberately weak ones is the model that wins most tabular prediction contests. Back to one feature here, so the sum can be drawn as a curve.

title: Ridge, Lasso, and Trees
text:
Fitting the Residuals




What each tree is given
Every tree after the first is fitted to what the ones before it got wrong.
What rises is the training \(R^2\): nothing before any tree, 0.66 after ten.
No one of these trees is a model. The sum of them is.

title: Ridge, Lasso, and Trees
text:
Important Hyperparameters


Number of trees
The only knob that keeps improving the training fit forever. Test R-squared peaks early — here, after about five.


Learning rate
How much of each tree is added. Small rates need more trees and usually end up better.


Depth
How much each tree may do on its own. Two or three is standard; the boosting is supposed to do the work.



Halve the learning rate and you roughly double the number of trees you need. Set the rate low, then stop adding trees when validation R-squared stops rising. Min observations per leaf is also important. We set it to 1 here for simplicity.

title: Ridge, Lasso, and Trees
text: Gradient Boosting

title: Ridge, Lasso, and Trees
text:
Every Boosting Hyperparameter


How much ensemble

n_estimators — how many trees
learning_rate — shrinkage per tree
subsample — rows per tree
loss — squared, absolute, huber
n_iter_no_change — early stopping


How much tree

max_depth — how deep

Three Varieties of Tools


Claude Code tools

Your own Python functions — run_python, or the valuation itself.


External MCP tools

title: DCF Valuation of Companies
text:
Where They Run







Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Grep
the agent’s own process — its filesystem, its shell, its network


Internal MCP tools
the same process — whatever it can import, it can run


External MCP tools
someone else’s server — arguments out over HTTP, only the result back


WebSearch
Anthropic’s search backend — titles and URLs, not pages


WebFetch
downloads from your machine, then a small model extracts what was asked




So “on your machine” holds for the filesystem and shell tools. The two web tools are not local: the search runs at Anthropic, and the fetched page is sent there to be read.

Agent Options







ClaudeAgentOptions





system_prompt
a string, or a file on disk when it is long


tools
which built-ins to include — tools=[] for none


disallowed_tools
takes a tool out of the model’s context entirely


allowed_tools
the tools that run without prompting


mcp_servers
the servers to connect, plus the one holding your tools


max_turns
how many tool-use round trips before the app stops it




allowed_tools is not a whitelist. A tool left off it still runs — it falls through to permission_mode.

title: DCF Valuation of Companies
text:
Permission Modes







permission_mode





default
prompts before file edits, shell commands, and network requests


acceptEdits
auto-approves edits and common filesystem commands


plan
read-only — proposes changes but makes none


dontAsk
only allowed_tools run; anything else is denied, not prompted


bypassPermissions
everything runs, no checks — sandboxed containers only

title: DCF Valuation of Companies
text:
Custom Tools
A Python function with a decorator giving its name, description, and arguments.
@tool(
    "get_financials",
    "Fetch a company's income statement, balance sheet and cash flow.",
    {"ticker": Annotated[str, "The stock's ticker symbol"]},
)
async def get_financials(args):
    t = yf.Ticker(args["ticker"])
    csv = t.income_stmt.to_csv()
    return {"content": [{"type": "text", "text": csv}]}
local_server = create_sdk_mcp_server(name="local", tools=[get_financials])

Tools fetch. The skill specifies the workbook, and the workbook’s own formulas do the arithmetic — so the valuation is not a tool.

title: DCF Valuation of Companies

Producing the Output


The workbook
The xlsx skill — pandas and openpyxl, plus a financial-modeling standard for formatting and formula conventions.


The deck
The pptx skill — markitdown and the pack scripts to edit a template, pptxgenjs under Node to build one from scratch.



The xlsx skill’s rule: formulas in the cells, not values computed in Python. =SUM(B2:B9), never the number Python got — so changing an assumption recalculates the workbook.
